title: The biscuit tin
text:
The map was folded inside an old exercise book at the bottom of Nenek’s wooden chest. My cousin Bayu found it while we were looking for her photo albums, and he held it up as if he had discovered gold.

“Laila, look! It’s a treasure map!”

It had been drawn in pencil, now faded to the colour of weak tea. There was the river, a square marked “market”, a circle labelled “kapok tree” and a line of tiny footprints leading to an X. Underneath, in careful joined-up writing, someone had written: “Twenty steps from the tree towards the water. Under the stone with the white stripe.”

“It’s probably a joke,” I said. But I was already reaching for my sandals.

The kapok tree was still there, taller than the map suggested, its roots spreading across the path like the knuckles of a giant hand. We counted twenty steps towards the river. Then we counted them again, because Bayu’s legs are much longer than mine and we had ended up in two different places.

It took us an hour to find the stone. It was half buried in mud, and its white stripe was hidden under a carpet of moss. When we finally lifted it, our hands were filthy and the afternoon light was turning gold. Underneath lay a rusty biscuit tin.

Inside, wrapped in plastic, were seven glass marbles, a hair clip shaped like a butterfly and a black-and-white photograph of three girls standing in front of the kapok tree. On the back, someone had written a date: 1968.

We ran all the way back to the house.

Nenek was shelling peanuts on the veranda. When she saw the tin, her hands stopped moving. She took the photograph and held it close to her face for a long time.

“This is Sri, and this is Tuti,” she said softly, touching each face with one finger. “And the girl with the crooked fringe is me.”

She told us that the three friends had buried the tin the year before Sri’s family moved to Sumatra. They had promised to dig it up together when they were grown up. Then Tuti moved to the city, Nenek got married, and the years slipped through their fingers like sand.

“We drew the map so that we would never forget,” she said. “And then I forgot.”

That evening, Ayah phoned some old neighbours, and by the next morning he had found Tuti’s number. Nenek said it was silly to get excited about an old biscuit tin. But I noticed that she put on her best kebaya before she dialled, and she kept the photograph on her lap the whole time.
